title: Coming into Focus
bodyHtml:
Paiwan is an Austronesian language spoken by around 66,000 people in southern Taiwan. One of the major components of Paiwan sentence structure is “focus,” which marks a new piece of information conveyed by the sentence. In English, we might represent this through phrasing, such as in sentence “It is the dog which the man likes”. In this example, the dog is focused.

Below are some sentences in Paiwan with their English translations. Sentence elements in bold are focused.

PaiwanEnglish
1. kanan nua uqaɬay tua kuka a quma nua tsakawThe man eats the chicken in the thief’s field.
2. tjmalaw tua vavuy a kuvatuMy dog angers the pig.
3. djavisen nua tsemas a kukamaThe spirit snatches my father.
4. sitarang nua uqaɬay a vuluqThe man protects (it) with the spear.
5. tjalawen nua suvavuy i tua umaq a aɬak nua vavaianYour pig angers the woman’s child in the house.
6. kman tua kuka a tsemasThe spirit eats the chicken.
7. djavisan nua pulingaw tua vuluq a gaduThe shaman snatches the spear in the mountain.
8. langedaen nua sivitay a qaya-qayamThe soldier hears the bird.

F1. How would you say these sentences in Paiwan?

  1. The man protects the field with the dog.
  2. Your shaman angers my bird in the spirit’s mountain.
  3. The woman snatches the pig.

Now look at the following question-answer dialogues. The first answer has been translated for you.

QuestionAnswer
9. inu a tmarang a tsakaw?tmarang a tsakaw i tua quma
The thief who protects (it) is in the field.
10. anema a sitjalaw nua sukama tua vatu?sitjalaw nua kukama tua vatu a kuvuluq
11. anema a sudjavisen?kudjavisen a qaya-qayam nua vavaian
12. inu a kanan nua uqaɬay?kanan nua uqaɬay a gadu

F2. Based on these examples, translate the following responses into English, underlining focused elements, and saying what questions (in Paiwan) could have prompted them.

  1. susitarang tua qaya-qayam nua pulingaw a tsemas
  2. kanen nua uqaɬay a vavuy i tua gadu
  3. kutjalawan tua suvatu a kuquma

(The letter pairs dj and tj each represent a single sound. The word langedaen in sentence 8 is actually langedain, but this was edited for the sake of simplicity.)

hints.text: Line up the eight sentences by which English phrase is in bold. Then compare the little words in front of each Paiwan noun (nua, tua, i tua, a) and the shape of the first word in the sentence. Both change depending on which element is focused.

The particle a always sits in front of the focused phrase, and the verb carries a marker that tells you what kind of thing is focused: doer, thing acted on, place, or tool. There are four different verb shapes in the data (an added -m-, a suffix, another suffix, and a prefix). Also watch for ku- and su- glued onto nouns and verbs: they mean “my/I” and “your/you”. A possessor is expressed with nua after the noun.

Try sentence 7 as practice: djavisan nua pulingaw tua vuluq a gadu = “The shaman snatches the spear in the mountain”, with the mountain focused. So djavis- “snatch” takes -an when the place is focused, the doer is nua pulingaw, the thing snatched is tua vuluq, and the focused place comes last after a. Compare that with sentence 3, where the thing snatched is focused instead, and note which part of the verb changes.

explanationHtml:
What “focus” means here

In Paiwan, exactly one phrase in the sentence is singled out as the new, highlighted information. That phrase is marked by the particle a, and the verb wears a badge saying what kind of role the highlighted phrase plays: the doer, the thing acted on, the place, or the instrument. English does something similar with “It is the dog that the man likes”, but English does not change the verb.

Step 1: the little words

Sort out the particles first. Every noun phrase has one:

  • a marks the focused phrase, and it comes last in the sentence.
  • nua marks the doer when the doer is not focused (sentence 3: nua tsemas “the spirit” does the snatching). It also marks a possessor: quma nua tsakaw “the thief’s field”.
  • tua marks the thing acted on when it is not focused (sentence 6: tua kuka “the chicken”).
  • i tua marks a place when the place is not focused (sentence 5: i tua umaq “in the house”).

Step 2: the four verb shapes

Now compare the verbs. The root for “anger” is tjalaw, for “eat” kan, for “snatch” djavis, for “protect” tarang, for “hear” langed.

  • Doer focused: an -m- is slipped in after the first consonant. kan becomes kman (6), tjalaw becomes tjmalaw (2), tarang becomes tmarang (9).
  • Thing acted on focused: suffix -en. djavisen (3), tjalawen (5), langedaen (8).
  • Place focused: suffix -an. kanan (1), djavisan (7).
  • Instrument focused: prefix si-. sitarang (4).

The word order is: verb, then the doer with nua, then the thing acted on with tua, then a non-focused place with i tua, and finally the focused phrase with a.

Step 3: my and your

ku- means “my” and su- means “your” when attached to a noun: kuvatu “my dog”, suvavuy “your pig”, kukama “my father”. Attached to a verb they name the doer instead: sudjavisen “you snatch (it)”, kudjavisen “I snatch (it)” — which is why no separate nua phrase is needed in sentence 11.

Building the F1 sentences

“The man protects the field with the dog”: the highlighted phrase is a tool, so use the si- verb; doer nua uqaɬay, thing protected tua quma, focused tool last with a. That gives sitarang nua uqaɬay tua quma a vatu.

“Your shaman angers my bird in the spirit’s mountain”: a place is focused, so tjalaw takes -an; then nua supulingaw, tua kuqaya-qayam, and finally a gadu nua tsemas (“mountain of the spirit”).

“The woman snatches the pig”: the doer is focused, so infix -m- into djavis, giving djmavis tua vavuy a vavaian.

The question-answer pairs

inu means “where” and anema means “what”. A question simply puts the question word where the focused phrase would be, using the matching verb form: inu a kanan nua uqaɬay? “Where does the man eat?” has the place-focus verb kanan, and the answer replaces inu with a gadu.

Notice one more thing in pairs 10 and 11: the question says “your” (su-) and the answer says “my/I” (ku-). That is just the ordinary conversational switch — what is “you” to the asker is “I” to the answerer. So to reconstruct a question from an answer, swap ku- and su-, replace the focused a phrase with anema (for a thing or tool) or inu (for a place), and keep the verb shape the same.

For example, kanen nua uqaɬay a vavuy i tua gadu has the -en verb, so the pig is the focused thing eaten: “The man eats the pig in the mountain.” The prompting question keeps kanen, keeps nua uqaɬay and i tua gadu, and starts with anema.

F2 items a, b, c each require TWO things (an English translation with the focused element underlined, plus a Paiwan question); the booklet prints one label per item, so each is transcribed as a single question whose answerKey holds both lines, graded by LLM. If the site's answer sheet splits these into separate translation and question blanks, the part may need to be re-split into six questions.
